title: Brightline Tech — Overtime classification problem
scenario: Brightline Tech, a fast-growing startup, classifies all of its customer-support representatives as 'exempt' salaried employees to simplify payroll. The reps routinely work 50–55 hours per week answering tickets and have no managerial duties.
context: Support reps have no supervisory authority and earn a fixed salary.
Reps regularly work more than 40 hours per week.
The company has never paid overtime.
A former employee has filed a complaint with the DOL.

questions.prompt: Why are the support reps likely misclassified under the FLSA?
options: They perform non-managerial duties and are not exempt, so they must be paid overtime
All salaried employees are automatically exempt
Salary amount alone determines exemption
Startups are exempt from the FLSA
questions.explanation: Exemption depends on job duties (and salary basis), not just being salaried. Workers with no managerial/professional duties are non-exempt and entitled to overtime.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate first step for HR to correct the problem?
options: Reclassify the reps as non-exempt and implement time tracking going forward
Fire the reps who complained
Ask reps to sign waivers of overtime
Ignore the DOL complaint
questions.explanation: HR should correct the classification, begin tracking hours, and pay overtime prospectively. Employees cannot waive FLSA rights.

questions.prompt: How should HR communicate the change to the affected reps?
options: Explain the correction transparently and set clear expectations for time tracking
Make the change quietly without explanation
Blame the employees for the error
Only tell managers
questions.explanation: Transparent communication builds trust and ensures compliance — employees need to understand the new classification and tracking requirements.

title: Harbor Health — Reasonable accommodation request
scenario: At Harbor Health, a medical-billing specialist develops a repetitive-strain injury and requests a voice-to-text software tool to continue entering billing codes. The manager wants to deny the request because the software costs money.
context: The employee is otherwise qualified for the role.
The requested software would cost under $1,000.
The manager is concerned about precedent and cost.
The employee can still perform the essential functions with the tool.

questions.prompt: What does the ADA require the employer to do here?
options: Engage in the interactive process to determine an effective accommodation
Deny the request because it costs money
Wait for a lawsuit before responding
Require the employee to pay for the software
questions.explanation: The ADA requires a good-faith interactive process to identify a reasonable accommodation; cost alone rarely justifies denial unless it is an undue hardship.

questions.prompt: Is a $1,000 software purchase likely an 'undue hardship' under the ADA?
options: No — undue hardship is assessed against the employer's resources, and this small cost is unlikely to qualify
Yes, any cost is an undue hardship
Yes, because it might set a precedent
Yes, because the manager said so
questions.explanation: Undue hardship considers significant difficulty or expense relative to the employer's size and resources. A small one-time cost is rarely an undue hardship.

questions.prompt: How should HR coach the manager who wants to deny the request?
options: Educate the manager on ADA obligations and the interactive process, focusing on the employee's ability to perform
Support the manager's instinct to deny to save money
Avoid the manager to prevent conflict
Tell the manager to make the decision alone
questions.explanation: HR should consult with the manager, explain the legal requirements, and guide a fair, individualized process rather than a cost-based reflex.

title: Summit Retail — Harassment complaint
scenario: A cashier at Summit Retail reports that a supervisor repeatedly makes sexual comments and has offered better shifts in exchange for dates. The employee says they fear retaliation for coming forward.
context: The complaint involves a supervisor, creating a power imbalance.
There are no witnesses to every incident.
The company has a written anti-harassment policy.

questions.prompt: What is HR's most appropriate first action?
options: Launch a prompt, impartial, and confidential investigation
Move the employee to another store without investigating
Tell the employee to resolve it with the supervisor
Dismiss the complaint because there are no witnesses
questions.explanation: Employers must promptly and impartially investigate harassment complaints; a supervisor's conduct is especially serious due to the power dynamic.

questions.prompt: How should the company protect the employee from retaliation?
options: Reassure the employee, monitor for retaliation, and prohibit any adverse action
Assume retaliation won't happen
Ask the supervisor to 'go easy' on the employee
Discourage the employee from escalating
questions.explanation: Retaliation is itself unlawful; employers must actively prevent and monitor for it, and communicate a clear non-retaliation policy.

questions.prompt: If the investigation substantiates the complaint, what is the appropriate outcome?
options: Take prompt, proportionate corrective action and document it
Take no action if the supervisor apologizes
Transfer the complainant and keep the supervisor in place
Wait to see if it recurs
questions.explanation: When harassment is substantiated, the employer must take prompt and effective corrective action to stop the behavior and prevent recurrence.

title: Cedar Grove — Rapid growth onboarding
scenario: Cedar Grove, a home-services company, doubled its workforce in six months. New hires are leaving within their first 90 days, and managers complain that new employees seem 'lost' and disengaged.
context: There is no structured onboarding program.
Turnover among new hires is high in the first 90 days.
Managers lack the time to train new employees individually.
The company needs to stabilize and retain its workforce.

questions.prompt: What is the most likely root cause of the 90-day turnover?
options: A lack of structured onboarding and role clarity
Generous compensation
Too much training
An over-staffed organization
questions.explanation: Poor onboarding and unclear expectations are leading causes of early turnover; new hires disengage when they feel unsupported.

questions.prompt: Which solution would best address the problem?
options: Implement a standardized onboarding program with clear milestones and manager check-ins
Hire more recruiters only
Reduce pay to save money
Extend the probation period
questions.explanation: A structured onboarding program with clear goals and regular check-ins integrates new hires and improves early retention.

questions.prompt: How should HR measure whether the new program is working?
options: Track 90-day turnover, time-to-productivity, and new-hire engagement scores
Ask managers for their gut feeling only
Ignore metrics and assume success
Measure only the number of hires
questions.explanation: Meaningful metrics — early turnover, time-to-productivity, and engagement — show whether onboarding is actually improving retention and performance.
